newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian communists press government over strike.
newsitem.headline: Indian communists press government over strike.

text.p: Communist parties backing Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda pressed the government on Thursday to bow to trade unions' demands as a nationwide strike disrupted telephone and postal services for the second day.
The two main communist parties came out in support of the unions' demands for the elimination of a ceiling on annual bonus payments.
Some one million telecommunications and postal workers launched an indefinite strike on Wednesday over the wage dispute.
Virtually all postal services were shut down, authorities said. Telecommunications services were only partially disrupted as most calls are routed through automatic exchanges.
The Communist Party of India (CPI), part of Deve Gowda's 13-party minority coalition, issued a statement expressing its solidarity with the striking workers.
The party said a 3,500 rupee ($100) ceiling on annual bonus payments had already been raised for port, dock and railway workers.
New Delhi normally pays most junior employees an annual bonus during the Hindu festive season starting in October.
The bonus is usually raised each year but the government this year decided not to raise the payment for telecommunications and postal employees as part of an austerity programme.
"The Communist Party of India urges the government to take an immediate decision so that the strike is not prolonged," the CPI statement said.

The separate Communist Party of India-Marxist, which backs Deve Gowda's government but is not part of the ruling coalition, said "there is no justification in retaining the ceiling on postal and telecom employees".
On Wednesday the government said it sympathised with the workers' demands but called the strike illegal and appealed to the workers to reconsider their decision.
"It's an illegal strike as they did not even give a 14-day notice to the government," Communications Minister Beni Prasad Varma told reporters on Wednesday.
In June last year, authorities called out troops to restore disrupted telephone services in a five-day strike by about 450,000 telecommunications workers.
The strike had been in protest against the government's moves to end a state monopoly on telephones.
